grammar.title: 3A: Choosing between comparatives and superlatives
grammar.explanation: Use a comparative adjective plus than to compare two people, places, or things, for example older than or more expensive than. Short adjectives add er: old becomes older, big becomes bigger, easy becomes easier. Longer adjectives use more: modern becomes more modern, difficult becomes more difficult. Some common adjectives are irregular: good becomes better, bad becomes worse, far becomes further or farther. Use not as plus adjective plus as to say two things are equal: as comfortable as, not as busy as. Use the plus a superlative to compare one person or thing with all of their group: the tallest, the most expensive, the best, the worst. After a superlative, use in, not of: the longest bridge in the world.
examples: My car is a bit older than yours.
Olive oil is better for you than butter.
The new sofa isn't as comfortable as the old one.
Kevin is the tallest player in the team.
Oslo is the most expensive capital city in Europe.
He drives more carefully than his girlfriend.
